### What happens if I lose a no-win-no-fee claim?
URL: https://jurimatch.com/guides/what-if-i-lose

Losing a no-win-no-fee claim usually means no fee for your own lawyer, but you may still face the other side's costs, expenses and insurance.

## Claim guides

### Claims against BBVA: floor clauses, mortgage costs and cards
URL: https://jurimatch.com/claims/bbva

BBVA is one of Spain's largest banks. It was among the banks in the case in which the Spanish Supreme Court first ruled on floor clauses in May 2013, and like other Spanish banks it has faced consumer claims over mortgage terms and credit products. This guide explains the usual claims and routes in Spain.

Q: Do I have to complain to BBVA before going to court?
A: In practice, yes. A written complaint to the bank's customer service is required before you can go to the Banco de España complaints service, and since April 2025 most civil claims in Spain require a prior attempt to settle. A documented written complaint usually serves both purposes.

Q: Do lawyers take these cases on a no-win-no-fee basis?
A: Many do, especially floor clause and mortgage expense claims, because when the bank loses in full it is normally ordered to pay costs. Ask for the fee agreement (hoja de encargo) in writing, including what happens if the bank settles early.

Q: Can I still claim if I have paid off the loan?
A: Often yes. Having repaid or cancelled a mortgage does not by itself prevent a claim about an unfair term, but any later agreement or waiver you signed needs to be reviewed.

### When a business partner takes the money: your options
URL: https://jurimatch.com/claims/business-partner-fraud

Partnership and shareholder disputes often start with exclusion from information and end with diverted revenue, dilution or asset stripping. Acting early protects both evidence and value.

Q: Can a shareholder dispute be funded?
A: Yes, where the business or stake is valuable enough. Funders and success-fee firms look at what can realistically be recovered or bought out.

### Claims against CaixaBank: mortgages, cards and former Bankia
URL: https://jurimatch.com/claims/caixabank

CaixaBank is one of Spain's largest banks and absorbed Bankia in 2021, so it is now the counterparty for many claims that began against Bankia. Like other Spanish banks, it has faced consumer claims over mortgage terms and credit products. This guide explains the usual claims and routes in Spain.

Q: Do I have to complain to CaixaBank before going to court?
A: In practice, yes. A written complaint to the bank's customer service is required before you can go to the Banco de España complaints service, and since April 2025 most civil claims in Spain require a prior attempt to settle. A documented written complaint usually serves both purposes.

Q: Do lawyers take these cases on a no-win-no-fee basis?
A: Many do, especially floor clause and mortgage expense claims, because when the bank loses in full it is normally ordered to pay costs. Ask for the fee agreement (hoja de encargo) in writing, including what happens if the bank settles early.

Q: Can I still claim if I have paid off the loan?
A: Often yes. Having repaid or cancelled a mortgage does not by itself prevent a claim about an unfair term, but any later agreement or waiver you signed needs to be reviewed.

### Crypto scam recovery: first steps and how lawyers trace funds
URL: https://jurimatch.com/claims/crypto-scam

Crypto transfers are public on the blockchain, which means funds can sometimes be followed to an exchange where an account holder can be identified. Speed matters: once funds are moved through mixers or off-ramped, options narrow.

Q: Can stolen crypto be recovered?
A: Sometimes, if the funds can be traced to an exchange or custodian that can be compelled to freeze and disclose account information. If funds were moved through mixers or to wallets nobody controls identifiably, recovery is much harder.

Q: Is there a no-win-no-fee option for crypto fraud?
A: Some firms work on success terms when tracing shows funds at an identifiable exchange. Initial tracing reports often carry a cost, so ask upfront what is included.

Q: How do I spot a recovery scam?
A: Unsolicited contact, upfront fees, claims of special access to blockchains or regulators, and pressure to act fast. Legitimate law firms are regulated and can be checked with the local bar or law society.

### Claims against easyJet: delays, cancellations and refunds
URL: https://jurimatch.com/claims/easyjet

easyJet operates through a UK company and separate European companies, so a flight can fall under the EU rules (EU261) or the UK rules (UK261) depending on the route and the operating carrier. Passenger claims are mostly about long delays, cancellations, refunds and baggage.

Q: Do I need a lawyer to claim compensation from easyJet?
A: Usually not for the first step: you can claim directly with the airline for free. A claim company or no-win-no-fee lawyer can help if the airline refuses or does not reply, in exchange for a share of the compensation.

Q: Does easyJet have to pay if the delay was caused by weather or strikes?
A: Not if the disruption was caused by extraordinary circumstances that could not have been avoided with reasonable measures, such as severe weather. Courts have held that strikes by the airline's own staff are not normally extraordinary, while strikes by third parties such as air traffic controllers can be. Each case depends on its facts.

Q: How much compensation can I get?
A: Under EU261 the fixed amounts are 250, 400 or 600 euros depending on distance (UK261 uses pounds). Our flight compensation calculator shows which band applies. Refunds and expenses for care are separate from compensation.

### Claims against Iberia: delays, cancellations and refunds
URL: https://jurimatch.com/claims/iberia

Iberia is a Spanish airline, so its flights are generally covered by EU Regulation 261/2004, including long-haul flights departing from Spain. Passenger claims are mostly about long delays, cancellations, missed connections, refunds and baggage.

Q: Do I need a lawyer to claim compensation from Iberia?
A: Usually not for the first step: you can claim directly with the airline for free. A claim company or no-win-no-fee lawyer can help if the airline refuses or does not reply, in exchange for a share of the compensation.

Q: Does Iberia have to pay if the delay was caused by weather or strikes?
A: Not if the disruption was caused by extraordinary circumstances that could not have been avoided with reasonable measures, such as severe weather. Courts have held that strikes by the airline's own staff are not normally extraordinary, while strikes by third parties such as air traffic controllers can be. Each case depends on its facts.

Q: How much compensation can I get?
A: Under EU261 the fixed amounts are 250, 400 or 600 euros depending on distance (UK261 uses pounds). Our flight compensation calculator shows which band applies. Refunds and expenses for care are separate from compensation.

### Insurance claim denied? How to challenge it
URL: https://jurimatch.com/claims/insurance-claim-denied

Insurers reject claims for many reasons, exclusions, late notification, alleged non-disclosure or disputes about the value of the loss. Many rejections can be challenged.

Q: Do lawyers take insurance disputes on a no-win-no-fee basis?
A: Often, because the insurer can pay. The main question is whether the policy wording supports your claim.

### Lost money to investment fraud? What to do first
URL: https://jurimatch.com/claims/investment-fraud

Investment fraud covers Ponzi schemes, fake funds, unauthorised trading, mis-sold products and advisers who misrepresented risk. The steps you take in the first weeks often decide whether money can still be traced and recovered.

Q: Can I get my money back from an investment scam?
A: Sometimes. It depends on whether the money can be traced, whether a solvent party (a bank, a regulated firm or an identifiable individual with assets) is responsible, and how quickly you act. A lawyer can tell you which of these applies to you.

Q: Do lawyers take investment fraud cases on a no-win-no-fee basis?
A: Many do, where recovery looks realistic, for example when a regulated entity or insurer is involved, or many investors were affected by the same scheme. Where it is less certain, firms may offer a reduced fee plus a success fee, or refer you to a litigation funder.

Q: Should I join a group claim?
A: Group or collective actions can share costs and make funding easier. Check who runs the claim, how fees are taken from any recovery, and whether you can leave.

### Claims against Lufthansa: delays, cancellations and refunds
URL: https://jurimatch.com/claims/lufthansa

Lufthansa is a German airline, so its flights are generally covered by EU Regulation 261/2004, including long-haul flights departing from the EU. Passenger claims are mostly about long delays, cancellations, missed connections, refunds and baggage. In Germany, independent conciliation bodies handle passenger disputes free of charge for passengers.

Q: Do I need a lawyer to claim compensation from Lufthansa?
A: Usually not for the first step: you can claim directly with the airline for free. A claim company or no-win-no-fee lawyer can help if the airline refuses or does not reply, in exchange for a share of the compensation.

Q: Does Lufthansa have to pay if the delay was caused by weather or strikes?
A: Not if the disruption was caused by extraordinary circumstances that could not have been avoided with reasonable measures, such as severe weather. Courts have held that strikes by the airline's own staff are not normally extraordinary, while strikes by third parties such as air traffic controllers can be. Each case depends on its facts.

Q: How much compensation can I get?
A: Under EU261 the fixed amounts are 250, 400 or 600 euros depending on distance (UK261 uses pounds). Our flight compensation calculator shows which band applies. Refunds and expenses for care are separate from compensation.

### Claims against Mercedes-Benz: diesel emissions
URL: https://jurimatch.com/claims/mercedes-benz

Owners of some Mercedes-Benz diesel cars have brought claims arguing that emissions controls worked differently on the road than in tests, for example through temperature-dependent settings. German authorities ordered recalls of some models, and the manufacturer has disputed that its vehicles contained unlawful defeat devices. This guide explains how these claims have generally worked.

Q: Is my Mercedes affected?
A: It depends on the engine, model and emissions class. Recall letters and official vehicle checkers are a starting point; a lawyer or claims group can check your specific car.

Q: How much could I get?
A: There is no fixed amount. In Germany, courts following the 2023 CJEU ruling have generally awarded a percentage of the purchase price for negligence claims; elsewhere it depends on national law and the claim.

Q: Do lawyers take these cases on a no-win-no-fee basis?
A: Many do, often backed by litigation funding or legal expenses insurance. Ask how the fee is calculated and what happens if the claim fails.

### Bad advice from a professional? Claiming for negligence
URL: https://jurimatch.com/claims/professional-negligence

Professionals owe a duty to act with reasonable skill and care. When they fall short and it causes a financial loss, you may have a claim, usually against their professional indemnity insurance.

Q: Who pays if I win a professional negligence claim?
A: Usually the professional's indemnity insurer, which is why these claims are often funded on success terms.

### Property and off-plan fraud: how to protect your claim
URL: https://jurimatch.com/claims/property-fraud

Property fraud ranges from fake listings and diverted deposits to off-plan developments that never complete and title problems discovered after purchase. Your contracts and payment records are the foundation of any claim.

Q: Can I recover a deposit from a developer that went bust?
A: Possibly, if your deposit was protected by a bank guarantee, escrow or insurance, or if directors can be held personally liable. Otherwise you may be an unsecured creditor in the insolvency.

Q: Do I need a lawyer in the country where the property is?
A: Usually yes, because property claims are generally governed by local law and heard by local courts.

### Romance and pig-butchering scams: what victims can do
URL: https://jurimatch.com/claims/romance-scam

Romance scams build trust over weeks or months, often before introducing an “investment” platform. Victims are not at fault, these are organised operations. There are practical steps that can still help.

Q: Will my bank refund a romance scam payment?
A: It depends on your country, how you paid and the bank's rules. Some countries have reimbursement schemes for authorised push-payment fraud. Report it to the bank immediately.

### Claims against Ryanair: delays, cancellations and refunds
URL: https://jurimatch.com/claims/ryanair

Ryanair is an Irish airline, so its flights from or to the EU are generally covered by EU Regulation 261/2004, and flights from the UK by UK261. Most passenger claims against it are about long delays, cancellations, refunds and baggage. This guide explains how those claims usually work.

### Claims against Santander: mortgages, cards and Banco Popular
URL: https://jurimatch.com/claims/santander

Banco Santander is one of Spain's largest banks and acquired Banco Popular in 2017. Like other Spanish banks, it has faced consumer claims over mortgage terms and credit products, and former Banco Popular investors brought claims after Popular's 2017 resolution. This guide explains the usual claims and routes in Spain.

Q: Do I have to complain to Santander before going to court?
A: In practice, yes. A written complaint to the bank's customer service is required before you can go to the Banco de España complaints service, and since April 2025 most civil claims in Spain require a prior attempt to settle. A documented written complaint usually serves both purposes.

### Client won't pay? A guide to recovering unpaid invoices
URL: https://jurimatch.com/claims/unpaid-invoices

Most unpaid invoices are resolved without court, but a structured approach, and acting before the debtor's position worsens, improves your chances.

Q: Will a lawyer recover a debt on a no-win-no-fee basis?
A: Many debt-recovery firms work for a percentage of what they collect, particularly for undisputed business debts.

Q: Can I claim interest and costs?
A: Many countries allow statutory interest and some recovery costs on late business payments. A lawyer can confirm what applies to your invoice.

### Claims against Volkswagen: the diesel emissions scandal
URL: https://jurimatch.com/claims/volkswagen

In September 2015 Volkswagen admitted that software in some of its diesel engines, mainly the EA189 engine used across the VW, Audi, SEAT and Skoda brands, made the cars perform differently in emissions tests than on the road. Owners in many countries have since brought individual and group claims. This guide explains how those claims have generally worked.

Q: Can I still claim against Volkswagen for dieselgate?
A: It depends on the country, the engine, when you bought the car and whether you joined a group action. In some countries ordinary deadlines for EA189 cars have passed; in others, or for other engines, claims may still be possible. Get a deadline check before anything else.

Q: Do I need to still own the car?
A: Not necessarily. Courts in some countries have allowed claims by buyers who have since sold the car, with the sale price taken into account.

Q: Do lawyers take diesel claims on a no-win-no-fee basis?
A: Many do, often with litigation funding or legal expenses insurance, because claims are numerous and similar. Read how the fee is calculated and what happens if you withdraw.

### Claims against Vueling: delays, cancellations and refunds
URL: https://jurimatch.com/claims/vueling

Vueling is a Spanish airline, so its flights are generally covered by EU Regulation 261/2004. Passenger claims against it are mostly about long delays, cancellations, missed connections, refunds and baggage. In Spain, the aviation safety agency AESA handles passenger complaints.

Q: How much compensation can I get?
A: Under EU261 the fixed amounts are 250, 400 or 600 euros depending on distance (UK261 uses pounds). Our flight compensation calculator shows which band applies. Refunds and expenses for care are separate from compensation.

## Fee comparisons

### Conditional fee agreement (CFA) vs After-the-event (ATE) insurance
URL: https://jurimatch.com/fees/cfa-vs-ate-insurance

They cover different risks and are often used together. A CFA means you pay your own solicitor no fee if you lose. ATE insurance pays the other side's costs, and often your own expenses, if you lose. A CFA alone leaves you exposed to the other side's costs.

Q: Do I need ATE insurance if I have a CFA?
A: Often yes, outside personal injury. A CFA only deals with your own solicitor's fees. If you lose, a court can still order you to pay the other side's costs, and ATE insurance is the usual protection.

Q: Who pays the ATE premium?
A: Usually you, out of your damages if you win. Many policies defer the premium and make it payable only if the claim succeeds, so nothing is due if you lose. Check the policy.

Q: Can my solicitor arrange ATE insurance?
A: Yes, solicitors usually arrange it with an insurer they work with. Ask what it covers, the limit of cover, the premium and when it is payable.

### Conditional fee agreement (CFA) vs Damages-based agreement (DBA)
URL: https://jurimatch.com/fees/cfa-vs-dba

Both mean you pay your own solicitor nothing if you lose. Under a CFA you pay normal fees plus a capped success fee if you win; under a DBA the solicitor takes a capped percentage of your damages instead. Neither covers the other side's costs, which is what ATE insurance is for.

Q: Is a CFA or a DBA cheaper?
A: It depends on the size of the damages and how much of the costs you recover. With high damages and low costs a CFA is often cheaper; with low recoverable costs a DBA can work out better. Ask the solicitor to model both on your figures.

Q: Do I pay anything if I lose under a CFA or DBA?
A: Not to your own solicitor, if the agreement says so. You may still owe disbursements such as court fees and experts, and the other side's costs unless you are protected (for example by QOCS in most personal injury claims) or insured with ATE insurance.

Q: Can a solicitor change from a CFA to a DBA mid-case?
A: Only by a new written agreement that you sign. Read how any work already done is treated before agreeing.

### Contingency fee vs Fixed fee
URL: https://jurimatch.com/fees/contingency-fee-vs-fixed-fee

A fixed fee is a set price agreed in advance and payable whatever the result. A contingency fee is a share of what you recover and nothing if you lose. Fixed fees suit simple, predictable work; contingency fees suit claims where you want the lawyer to share the risk.

Q: Can I combine a fixed fee and a success fee?
A: Often, yes. Many lawyers in Spain, France, Italy and Brazil charge a smaller fixed fee plus a success fee. In some countries this mix is the only form allowed.

Q: What does a fixed fee usually not include?
A: Court fees, expert reports and the other side's costs if you lose. Ask exactly which steps the fixed fee covers and what happens if the case goes further, such as to an appeal.

Q: Is a contingency fee always more expensive if I win?
A: Not always. It depends on the size of the award and how much work the case needs. Ask the lawyer to show you both options on your figures.

### Contingency fee vs Litigation funding
URL: https://jurimatch.com/fees/contingency-fee-vs-litigation-funding

With a contingency fee your own lawyer works without being paid unless you recover. With litigation funding a separate company pays the legal costs, and often the risk of the other side's costs, in return for a share of the recovery. Funders usually look for larger claims.

Q: Can I use a contingency fee and litigation funding together?
A: Sometimes. A funder may pay part of the costs while the law firm takes a reduced fee plus a success element. The total taken from your recovery should be set out in writing before you sign.

Q: Do I have to repay a litigation funder if I lose?
A: Normally not: most funding is non-recourse, so the funder loses its investment. Check the agreement for exceptions such as misconduct or abandoning the case.

Q: Which leaves me more money if I win?
A: It depends on the percentages, the length of the case and the multiple the funder charges. Ask for a worked example at several outcomes and timelines.

### No win, no fee vs Hourly fees
URL: https://jurimatch.com/fees/no-win-no-fee-vs-hourly-fees

Under no win, no fee you pay your own lawyer nothing if you lose, but give up a share of a win. Paying by the hour costs money whatever the outcome, but you keep the whole award. No win, no fee suits claimants who cannot or do not want to fund the risk.

Q: Is no win no fee really free if I lose?
A: You pay your own lawyer nothing if the agreement says so, but you may still owe expenses such as court fees and experts, and in most countries outside the US the other side's costs. Ask who covers these before signing.

Q: Why would a lawyer turn down my case on no win no fee?
A: Because they are taking the risk. Lawyers look at the chances of winning, the amount at stake, whether the other side can pay, and the time it will take.

Q: Can I switch from hourly fees to no win no fee?
A: Sometimes, with a new written agreement. A new firm may also take over a case on success terms after reviewing it.

### JuriMatch, claims management companies and lawyers: the differences
URL: https://jurimatch.com/vs/claims-management-companies

A claims management company handles a claim for you, usually for a share of the compensation, but is not a law firm. A lawyer can advise you and go to court. JuriMatch is neither: it is a directory and search engine that helps you find lawyers and funders, and does not take a share of your compensation.

Q: Is JuriMatch a claims management company?
A: No. JuriMatch does not handle claims and does not take a share of compensation. It is a directory and search engine that helps you find no-win-no-fee lawyers and litigation funders, plus free guides and tools.

Q: Can I make a claim without a claims management company?
A: Often yes. Flight compensation, many consumer complaints and complaints about financial services can be made directly to the company and then to an ombudsman or alternative dispute resolution body, free of charge.

Q: Who regulates claims management companies?
A: In Great Britain, the Financial Conduct Authority has regulated claims management activity since 1 April 2019. Rules differ in other countries, and in many there is no specific regulator for claims companies.

### No-win-no-fee lawyer vs legal aid
URL: https://jurimatch.com/vs/no-win-no-fee-vs-legal-aid

Legal aid is paid by the state for people with limited means, and usually also requires a case with reasonable merit. A no-win-no-fee lawyer is paid from what you recover, whatever your income. If you might qualify for legal aid, check first: it can also cover court fees.

Q: Who qualifies for justicia gratuita in Spain?
A: Ley 1/1996 sets income limits linked to the IPREM index: broadly up to twice the IPREM for individuals, more for family units. Other factors, such as assets and the type of case, also count. The bar association's legal aid service can confirm whether you qualify.

Q: Does legal aid in England and Wales cover money claims?
A: Mostly not. Since the Legal Aid, Sentencing and Punishment of Offenders Act 2012, most civil money claims, including most personal injury, debt and employment claims, are outside the scope of legal aid. Conditional fee agreements and damages-based agreements are the usual alternatives.

Q: If I get legal aid and lose, do I pay the other side's costs?
A: It depends on the country. In Germany, Prozesskostenhilfe does not protect you from paying the winner's costs. In other systems the protection is wider. Ask the legal aid service or your assigned lawyer before the case starts.

### No-win-no-fee lawyer vs legal expenses insurance
URL: https://jurimatch.com/vs/no-win-no-fee-vs-legal-expenses-insurance

Legal expenses insurance is a policy you buy before a dispute starts; if the dispute is covered, the insurer pays legal costs up to a limit. A no-win-no-fee lawyer is paid from what you win. Check for existing cover first: many home, car and bank policies include it.

Q: Do I already have legal expenses insurance?
A: Possibly. It is often included as an add-on to home, car or bank account policies, especially in Germany, Austria and several other European countries. Check your policy documents or ask your insurer before paying a lawyer.

Q: Can my legal expenses insurer force me to use its lawyer?
A: In the EU, Article 201 of Directive 2009/138/EC gives you a free choice of lawyer for any inquiry or proceedings, and whenever there is a conflict of interest; the Court of Justice has read this right broadly. Before that point, the insurer may handle the claim itself or use a panel firm.

Q: Can I use both legal expenses insurance and a no-win-no-fee lawyer?
A: Sometimes. If the insurance limit is lower than the expected costs, a lawyer may agree success-based terms for the part the policy does not pay. Ask both the insurer and the lawyer to confirm in writing how they would work together.

Q: Does legal expenses insurance cover a dispute that started before I bought it?
A: Normally not. Policies usually exclude disputes whose cause arose before the cover began, and many apply a waiting period after purchase.

## Glossary

### No-win-no-fee terms, explained
URL: https://jurimatch.com/glossary

Plain-language definitions of no-win-no-fee terms: contingency fee, CFA, DBA, ATE insurance, litigation funding, cuota litis, Erfolgshonorar and more…

Q: What is No win, no fee?
A: An arrangement where you do not pay your own lawyer's fees if the case is lost. If you win, the lawyer is paid from the result or recovers fees from the other side. Court fees, expert costs and the other side's costs may still apply, so read the agreement.

Q: What is Contingency fee?
A: The lawyer's fee is a percentage of the money recovered and nothing is due if there is no recovery. The percentage, and whether expenses are deducted before or after it, is set in the written agreement and is limited by local rules in some places.

Q: What is Conditional fee agreement (CFA)?
A: The lawyer charges normal fees only if you win, plus a success fee on top of those fees. The success fee cannot exceed 100% of the base costs, and in personal injury claims it is capped at 25% of certain damages.

Q: What is Damages-based agreement (DBA)?
A: The lawyer takes a percentage of the damages you recover instead of hourly fees. The cap, including VAT, is 25% in personal injury claims, 35% in employment claims and 50% in other claims.

Q: What is After-the-event (ATE) insurance?
A: Insurance bought after a dispute arises that pays the other side's costs, and often your own expenses, if you lose. The premium is frequently deferred and payable only if you win.

Q: What is Adverse costs (loser pays)?
A: The rule that the losing party pays part of the winner's legal costs. It is why a no-win-no-fee agreement with your own lawyer does not always mean you risk nothing.

Q: What is Litigation funding (third-party funding)?
A: A company that is not a party to the case pays the legal costs in exchange for a share of the money recovered. Funding is usually non-recourse: if the case is lost, you do not repay the funder.

Q: What is Cuota litis?
A: An agreement where the lawyer's fee depends on the result, usually a percentage of what is obtained. In Spain the professional ban on it was struck down by the Supreme Court in 2008, so it can be agreed freely in writing.

Q: What is Patto di quota lite?
A: An agreement giving the lawyer a share of the asset or sum in dispute. Since 2012 Italian law forbids it again, but a fee calculated as a percentage of the value of the case, agreed in writing in advance, is allowed.

Q: What is Erfolgshonorar?
A: A fee that depends on success. It is generally not allowed for lawyers, with exceptions: for example claims of up to 2,000 euros, certain debt collection work, and cases where the client could not otherwise afford to bring the claim.

Q: What is Honoraire de résultat?
A: A bonus linked to the result. A fee based only on the result (pacte de quota litis) is not allowed, but a result-based fee can be added to a fixed or hourly fee if it is agreed in writing.

Q: What is Success fee?
A: Any fee, or part of a fee, that is payable only if the case succeeds. How it is calculated, and whether it is allowed at all, depends on the country.

Q: What is Limitation period?
A: The deadline for starting a claim. Once it has passed the claim is usually barred, so check it early; periods differ by country and type of claim and can be paused or restarted in some situations.

Q: What is Legal expenses insurance (BTE)?
A: Insurance bought before any dispute arises ("before the event"), often included in home, car or bank policies, that pays legal costs if a covered dispute comes up. Check your policies before agreeing anything else: the insurer may have to approve the lawyer and the costs.

Q: What is Qualified one-way costs shifting (QOCS)?
A: A rule for most personal injury claims under which a claimant who loses is generally not ordered to pay the defendant's costs out of their own pocket. Costs orders can still be set off against damages, and the protection can be lost, for example if the claim is found to be fundamentally dishonest.

Q: What is Disbursements?
A: Expenses a lawyer pays to third parties while running your case, such as court fees, expert reports, medical records and translations. Some no-win-no-fee agreements cover them if you lose; others make you pay them whatever the result. The agreement should say which.

Q: What is Class action?
A: A single case brought by one or more representatives on behalf of a larger group with similar claims. Members are often included unless they opt out, and any settlement usually needs the court's approval. Lawyers in class actions are frequently paid on a contingency basis.

Q: What is EU representative action?
A: A collective action brought by an approved organisation (a "qualified entity") on behalf of consumers, under Directive (EU) 2020/1828, to stop an unlawful practice or obtain redress. Each member state sets its own details, including whether consumers opt in or opt out.

Q: What is Group litigation order (GLO)?
A: A court order that manages many separate claims raising common issues together. Claimants usually join by being entered on a group register, and decisions on the common issues bind the claims on the register.

Q: What is Letter before action?
A: A formal letter to the other side setting out the claim, what you want and a deadline to respond, sent before starting court proceedings. Courts expect it, and skipping it can affect who pays the costs. Our free claim letter tool helps you draft one.

Q: What is Statute of limitations?
A: The US name for the law that sets the deadline for filing a lawsuit. Each state sets its own periods by type of claim, and federal claims have their own, so the same claim can have different deadlines in different states.

Q: What is Small claims procedure?
A: A simpler and cheaper court procedure for low-value claims, designed so that people can bring a claim without a lawyer. The value limit and the costs rules differ by country; in England and Wales the small claims track generally covers claims up to £10,000.

Q: What is Out-of-court settlement?
A: An agreement that ends a dispute without a court judgment, usually in exchange for a payment. Most claims settle. On a no-win-no-fee agreement, a settlement normally counts as a win, so the lawyer's success fee or percentage applies to the amount agreed.

Q: What is Burofax?
A: A certified communication sent through the Spanish postal service with proof of content and delivery. It is commonly used to send a formal demand before a claim, and a demand received by the debtor can interrupt the limitation period.

Q: What is Proceso monitorio?
A: A fast Spanish court procedure to recover a money debt backed by documents, such as invoices or a signed contract. The initial application can be filed without a lawyer. If the debtor does not pay or object, the court can order enforcement.

Q: What is European order for payment?
A: A procedure under Regulation (EC) No 1896/2006 to recover uncontested money claims across EU borders using standard forms. If the debtor does not object, the order becomes enforceable in the other member states.

Q: What is European Small Claims Procedure?
A: A written procedure for cross-border claims of up to €5,000 under Regulation (EC) No 861/2007, using standard forms and usually without a hearing. A lawyer is not required.

Q: What is Funding multiple?
A: A way of setting a litigation funder's return as a multiple of the money it invests in the case, often compared with, or combined with, a percentage of the recovery. The funding agreement should state how the return is calculated and in what order the proceeds are paid out.

Q: What is Non-recourse funding?
A: Funding that is repaid only out of what the case recovers. If the case is lost, you owe the funder nothing. Most third-party litigation funding works this way, but check whether the agreement also covers the other side's costs.

Q: What is Security for costs?
A: An order requiring a claimant to pay money into court or give a guarantee to cover the defendant's costs if the claim fails, for example when the claimant lives abroad or is a company that may not be able to pay. Funders and ATE insurers can sometimes provide it.

Q: What is Pactum de quota litis?
A: Latin for an agreement under which a lawyer's fee is only a share of what the client wins. Many civil-law countries forbid it while allowing a success bonus on top of a base fee; Spain has allowed it since 2008.

Q: What is Honorários de êxito?
A: A success fee agreed between client and lawyer, often alongside a smaller fixed fee. It is separate from the honorários de sucumbência, the costs a court orders the losing side to pay to the winner's lawyer.

Q: What is Prozessfinanzierung?
A: The German term for third-party litigation funding: a funder pays the court and lawyer costs, and the other side's costs if the case is lost, in return for a share of the proceeds agreed in the contract. Funders usually look for larger claims with good prospects.

Q: What is No foil, no fee?
A: The Irish form of no-win-no-fee: the solicitor charges no fee if the case is lost. Irish solicitors may not charge a percentage of the damages, and you may still face the other side's costs if you lose.

Q: What is Claims management company (CMC)?
A: A business that handles claims for a share of the compensation, often passing them to a law firm. In Great Britain, CMCs have been regulated by the Financial Conduct Authority since 2019. Many claims can be made directly for free, so check before signing.

Q: What is Costs follow the event?
A: The general principle that the losing party pays the winning party's legal costs, usually only part of them, as assessed by the court. Courts can depart from it, for example when the winner behaved unreasonably.

Q: What is American rule on costs?
A: The principle that each side pays its own lawyer whatever the result, unless a statute or contract says otherwise. It is one reason contingency fees work well in the US: losing usually does not mean paying the other side's lawyer.

Q: What is Disclosure of documents?
A: The stage of a case in which each side must reveal relevant documents, including some that harm its own case. It can be costly and time-consuming, which is one reason lawyers and funders weigh it when deciding whether to take a case.

Q: What is Late payment interest?
A: Statutory interest a business can charge on late payment by another business. Under the EU Late Payment Directive the rate is at least 8 percentage points above the reference rate, plus a fixed €40 compensation per invoice; the UK has its own similar rules. Our free calculator works it out.

Q: What is EU261 flight compensation?
A: Fixed compensation under Regulation (EC) No 261/2004 of €250, €400 or €600 depending on flight distance, for long delays at arrival, late cancellations and denied boarding, unless the airline proves extraordinary circumstances. The UK version pays similar amounts in pounds.

### Adverse costs (loser pays)
URL: https://jurimatch.com/glossary/adverse-costs

The rule that the losing party pays part of the winner's legal costs. It is why a no-win-no-fee agreement with your own lawyer does not always mean you risk nothing.

Q: What is Adverse costs?
A: The rule that the losing party pays part of the winner's legal costs. It is why a no-win-no-fee agreement with your own lawyer does not always mean you risk nothing.

Q: Where is the term used?
A: Mainly in Most countries outside the United States.

A: Mainly in Mainly England and Wales.

A: A formal letter to the other side setting out the claim, what you want and a deadline to respond, sent before starting court proceedings. Courts expect it, and skipping it can affect who pays the costs. Our free claim letter tool helps you draft one.

Q: Where is the term used?
A: Mainly in England and Wales, and similar formal demand letters elsewhere.

### Limitation period
URL: https://jurimatch.com/glossary/limitation-period

The deadline for starting a claim. Once it has passed the claim is usually barred, so check it early; periods differ by country and type of claim and can be paused or restarted in some situations.

Q: What is Limitation period?
A: The deadline for starting a claim. Once it has passed the claim is usually barred, so check it early; periods differ by country and type of claim and can be paused or restarted in some situations.

Q: Where is the term used?
A: It is a general term, used in many countries.

### Litigation funding (third-party funding)
URL: https://jurimatch.com/glossary/litigation-funding

A company that is not a party to the case pays the legal costs in exchange for a share of the money recovered. Funding is usually non-recourse: if the case is lost, you do not repay the funder.

Q: What is Litigation funding?
A: A company that is not a party to the case pays the legal costs in exchange for a share of the money recovered. Funding is usually non-recourse: if the case is lost, you do not repay the funder.

Q: Where is the term used?
A: It is a general term, used in many countries.

### No foil, no fee
URL: https://jurimatch.com/glossary/no-foil-no-fee

The Irish form of no-win-no-fee: the solicitor charges no fee if the case is lost. Irish solicitors may not charge a percentage of the damages, and you may still face the other side's costs if you lose.

Q: What is No foil, no fee?
A: The Irish form of no-win-no-fee: the solicitor charges no fee if the case is lost. Irish solicitors may not charge a percentage of the damages, and you may still face the other side's costs if you lose.

Q: Where is the term used?
A: Mainly in Ireland.

### No win, no fee
URL: https://jurimatch.com/glossary/no-win-no-fee

An arrangement where you do not pay your own lawyer's fees if the case is lost. If you win, the lawyer is paid from the result or recovers fees from the other side. Court fees, expert costs and the other side's costs may still apply, so read the agreement.

Q: What is No win, no fee?
A: An arrangement where you do not pay your own lawyer's fees if the case is lost. If you win, the lawyer is paid from the result or recovers fees from the other side. Court fees, expert costs and the other side's costs may still apply, so read the agreement.

Q: Where is the term used?
A: It is a general term, used in many countries.

### Non-recourse funding
URL: https://jurimatch.com/glossary/non-recourse-funding

Funding that is repaid only out of what the case recovers. If the case is lost, you owe the funder nothing. Most third-party litigation funding works this way, but check whether the agreement also covers the other side's costs.

Q: What is Non-recourse funding?
A: Funding that is repaid only out of what the case recovers. If the case is lost, you owe the funder nothing. Most third-party litigation funding works this way, but check whether the agreement also covers the other side's costs.

Q: Where is the term used?
A: It is a general term, used in many countries.

### Out-of-court settlement
URL: https://jurimatch.com/glossary/out-of-court-settlement

An agreement that ends a dispute without a court judgment, usually in exchange for a payment. Most claims settle. On a no-win-no-fee agreement, a settlement normally counts as a win, so the lawyer's success fee or percentage applies to the amount agreed.

Q: What is Out-of-court settlement?
A: An agreement that ends a dispute without a court judgment, usually in exchange for a payment. Most claims settle. On a no-win-no-fee agreement, a settlement normally counts as a win, so the lawyer's success fee or percentage applies to the amount agreed.

Q: Where is the term used?
A: It is a general term, used in many countries.

### Pactum de quota litis
URL: https://jurimatch.com/glossary/pactum-de-quota-litis

Latin for an agreement under which a lawyer's fee is only a share of what the client wins. Many civil-law countries forbid it while allowing a success bonus on top of a base fee; Spain has allowed it since 2008.

Q: What is Pactum de quota litis?
A: Latin for an agreement under which a lawyer's fee is only a share of what the client wins. Many civil-law countries forbid it while allowing a success bonus on top of a base fee; Spain has allowed it since 2008.

Q: Where is the term used?
A: Mainly in Civil-law countries.

### Proceso monitorio
URL: https://jurimatch.com/glossary/proceso-monitorio

A fast Spanish court procedure to recover a money debt backed by documents, such as invoices or a signed contract. The initial application can be filed without a lawyer. If the debtor does not pay or object, the court can order enforcement.

Q: What is Proceso monitorio?
A: A fast Spanish court procedure to recover a money debt backed by documents, such as invoices or a signed contract. The initial application can be filed without a lawyer. If the debtor does not pay or object, the court can order enforcement.

Q: Where is the term used?
A: Mainly in Spain.

### Prozessfinanzierung
URL: https://jurimatch.com/glossary/prozessfinanzierung

The German term for third-party litigation funding: a funder pays the court and lawyer costs, and the other side's costs if the case is lost, in return for a share of the proceeds agreed in the contract. Funders usually look for larger claims with good prospects.

Q: What is Prozessfinanzierung?
A: The German term for third-party litigation funding: a funder pays the court and lawyer costs, and the other side's costs if the case is lost, in return for a share of the proceeds agreed in the contract. Funders usually look for larger claims with good prospects.

Q: Where is the term used?
A: Mainly in Germany, Austria and Switzerland.

### Qualified one-way costs shifting (QOCS)
URL: https://jurimatch.com/glossary/qualified-one-way-costs-shifting

A rule for most personal injury claims under which a claimant who loses is generally not ordered to pay the defendant's costs out of their own pocket. Costs orders can still be set off against damages, and the protection can be lost, for example if the claim is found to be fundamentally dishonest.

Q: What is Qualified one-way costs shifting?
A: A rule for most personal injury claims under which a claimant who loses is generally not ordered to pay the defendant's costs out of their own pocket. Costs orders can still be set off against damages, and the protection can be lost, for example if the claim is found to be fundamentally dishonest.

Q: Where is the term used?
A: Mainly in England and Wales.

### Patto di quota lite
URL: https://jurimatch.com/glossary/quota-lite

An agreement giving the lawyer a share of the asset or sum in dispute. Since 2012 Italian law forbids it again, but a fee calculated as a percentage of the value of the case, agreed in writing in advance, is allowed.

Q: What is Patto di quota lite?
A: An agreement giving the lawyer a share of the asset or sum in dispute. Since 2012 Italian law forbids it again, but a fee calculated as a percentage of the value of the case, agreed in writing in advance, is allowed.

Q: Where is the term used?
A: Mainly in Italy.

### Security for costs
URL: https://jurimatch.com/glossary/security-for-costs

An order requiring a claimant to pay money into court or give a guarantee to cover the defendant's costs if the claim fails, for example when the claimant lives abroad or is a company that may not be able to pay. Funders and ATE insurers can sometimes provide it.

Q: What is Security for costs?
A: An order requiring a claimant to pay money into court or give a guarantee to cover the defendant's costs if the claim fails, for example when the claimant lives abroad or is a company that may not be able to pay. Funders and ATE insurers can sometimes provide it.

Q: Where is the term used?
A: Mainly in England and Wales, Ireland, Australia and other common-law systems.

### Small claims procedure
URL: https://jurimatch.com/glossary/small-claims-procedure

A simpler and cheaper court procedure for low-value claims, designed so that people can bring a claim without a lawyer. The value limit and the costs rules differ by country; in England and Wales the small claims track generally covers claims up to £10,000.

Q: What is Small claims procedure?
A: A simpler and cheaper court procedure for low-value claims, designed so that people can bring a claim without a lawyer. The value limit and the costs rules differ by country; in England and Wales the small claims track generally covers claims up to £10,000.

Q: Where is the term used?
A: It is a general term, used in many countries.

### Statute of limitations
URL: https://jurimatch.com/glossary/statute-of-limitations

The US name for the law that sets the deadline for filing a lawsuit. Each state sets its own periods by type of claim, and federal claims have their own, so the same claim can have different deadlines in different states.

Q: What is Statute of limitations?
A: The US name for the law that sets the deadline for filing a lawsuit. Each state sets its own periods by type of claim, and federal claims have their own, so the same claim can have different deadlines in different states.

Q: Where is the term used?
A: Mainly in United States.

### Success fee
URL: https://jurimatch.com/glossary/success-fee

Any fee, or part of a fee, that is payable only if the case succeeds. How it is calculated, and whether it is allowed at all, depends on the country.

Q: What is Success fee?
A: Any fee, or part of a fee, that is payable only if the case succeeds. How it is calculated, and whether it is allowed at all, depends on the country.

Q: Where is the term used?
A: It is a general term, used in many countries.

## Country comparisons

### Argentina vs Chile: claim rules compared
URL: https://jurimatch.com/compare-countries/argentina-vs-chile

Contract claims, indicative limitation period: Argentina 5 years, Chile 5 years. In most countries outside the United States, a court can order the losing party to pay at least part of the winner's legal costs. General information, not legal advice.

### Australia vs New Zealand: claim rules compared
URL: https://jurimatch.com/compare-countries/australia-vs-new-zealand

Contract claims, indicative limitation period: Australia 3–6 years, New Zealand 6 years. The loser is usually ordered to pay a portion of the winner's legal costs, so ask your firm who carries that risk on a no-win-no-fee agreement.. General information, not legal advice.

### Belgium vs Luxembourg: claim rules compared
URL: https://jurimatch.com/compare-countries/belgium-vs-luxembourg

Contract claims, indicative limitation period: Belgium 10 years, Luxembourg 10–30 years. The loser pays the court costs and a fixed procedural indemnity towards the winner's lawyer fees, set within statutory brackets according to the value of the claim.. General information, not legal advice.

### France vs Belgium: claim rules compared
URL: https://jurimatch.com/compare-countries/france-vs-belgium

Contract claims, indicative limitation period: France 5 years (from knowledge), Belgium 10 years. The loser usually pays the court costs (dépens), and the judge may order a contribution to the winner's lawyer fees (article 700), which is often well below the real fees.. General information, not legal advice.

### France vs Germany: claim rules compared
URL: https://jurimatch.com/compare-countries/france-vs-germany

Contract claims, indicative limitation period: France 5 years (from knowledge), Germany 3 years (from knowledge). The loser usually pays the court costs (dépens), and the judge may order a contribution to the winner's lawyer fees (article 700), which is often well below the real fees.. General information, not legal advice.

### France vs Italy: claim rules compared
URL: https://jurimatch.com/compare-countries/france-vs-italy

Contract claims, indicative limitation period: France 5 years (from knowledge), Italy 10 years. The loser usually pays the court costs (dépens), and the judge may order a contribution to the winner's lawyer fees (article 700), which is often well below the real fees.. General information, not legal advice.

### France vs Switzerland: claim rules compared
URL: https://jurimatch.com/compare-countries/france-vs-switzerland

Contract claims, indicative limitation period: France 5 years (from knowledge), Switzerland 5–10 years. The loser usually pays the court costs (dépens), and the judge may order a contribution to the winner's lawyer fees (article 700), which is often well below the real fees.. General information, not legal advice.

### Germany vs Austria: claim rules compared
URL: https://jurimatch.com/compare-countries/germany-vs-austria

Contract claims, indicative limitation period: Germany 3 years (from knowledge), Austria 3–30 years. The loser pays the court fees and both sides' statutory lawyer fees, so the risk can be calculated in advance from the value of the claim. General information, not legal advice.

### Germany vs Denmark: claim rules compared
URL: https://jurimatch.com/compare-countries/germany-vs-denmark

Contract claims, indicative limitation period: Germany 3 years (from knowledge), Denmark 3 years (from knowledge). The loser pays the court fees and both sides' statutory lawyer fees, so the risk can be calculated in advance from the value of the claim. General information, not legal advice.

### Germany vs Netherlands: claim rules compared
URL: https://jurimatch.com/compare-countries/germany-vs-netherlands

Contract claims, indicative limitation period: Germany 3 years (from knowledge), Netherlands 5 years. The loser pays the court fees and both sides' statutory lawyer fees, so the risk can be calculated in advance from the value of the claim. General information, not legal advice.

### Germany vs Poland: claim rules compared
URL: https://jurimatch.com/compare-countries/germany-vs-poland

Contract claims, indicative limitation period: Germany 3 years (from knowledge), Poland 3–6 years. The loser pays the court fees and both sides' statutory lawyer fees, so the risk can be calculated in advance from the value of the claim. General information, not legal advice.

### Germany vs Switzerland: claim rules compared
URL: https://jurimatch.com/compare-countries/germany-vs-switzerland

Contract claims, indicative limitation period: Germany 3 years (from knowledge), Switzerland 5–10 years. The loser pays the court fees and both sides' statutory lawyer fees, so the risk can be calculated in advance from the value of the claim. General information, not legal advice.

### Netherlands vs Belgium: claim rules compared
URL: https://jurimatch.com/compare-countries/netherlands-vs-belgium

Contract claims, indicative limitation period: Netherlands 5 years, Belgium 10 years. The loser usually pays a fixed-rate contribution to the winner's costs (liquidatietarief), which is normally much lower than the real cost of the case.. General information, not legal advice.

### Spain vs France: claim rules compared
URL: https://jurimatch.com/compare-countries/spain-vs-france

Contract claims, indicative limitation period: Spain 5 years, France 5 years (from knowledge). The loser is normally ordered to pay the costs (condena en costas) unless the case raised serious doubts. General information, not legal advice.

### Spain vs Portugal: claim rules compared
URL: https://jurimatch.com/compare-countries/spain-vs-portugal

Contract claims, indicative limitation period: Spain 5 years, Portugal 20 years. The loser is normally ordered to pay the costs (condena en costas) unless the case raised serious doubts. General information, not legal advice.

### Sweden vs Finland: claim rules compared
URL: https://jurimatch.com/compare-countries/sweden-vs-finland

Contract claims, indicative limitation period: Sweden 10 years, Finland 3 years. The loser is normally ordered to pay the winner's reasonable legal costs. General information, not legal advice.

### Sweden vs Norway: claim rules compared
URL: https://jurimatch.com/compare-countries/sweden-vs-norway

Contract claims, indicative limitation period: Sweden 10 years, Norway 3 years. The loser is normally ordered to pay the winner's reasonable legal costs. General information, not legal advice.

### United Kingdom vs Ireland: claim rules compared
URL: https://jurimatch.com/compare-countries/united-kingdom-vs-ireland

Contract claims, indicative limitation period: United Kingdom 6 years, Ireland 6 years. In England & Wales the loser is normally ordered to pay a large part of the winner's costs. General information, not legal advice.

### United States vs Canada: claim rules compared
URL: https://jurimatch.com/compare-countries/united-states-vs-canada

Contract claims, indicative limitation period: United States 3–6 years, Canada 2–3 years (from knowledge). Each side normally pays its own lawyer (the "American rule"), so losing usually does not mean paying the other side's lawyer. General information, not legal advice.

### United States vs Mexico: claim rules compared
URL: https://jurimatch.com/compare-countries/united-states-vs-mexico

Contract claims, indicative limitation period: United States 3–6 years, Mexico Varies, ask a lawyer. Each side normally pays its own lawyer (the "American rule"), so losing usually does not mean paying the other side's lawyer. General information, not legal advice.
